description: We’re building a web tool for “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” using NASA data (MERRA-2, GPM, MODIS). It maps regional trends over time and shows what is changing, where, how much, and whether it’s statistically significant, with plain-language summaries. Looking for teammates in data/statistics (Python), Earth science, UI design, and presentation. We’re students from Karachi working remotely. Beginners welcome!
summary:
Sherlock Earth is an interactive web tool that shows what is changing on Earth, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. We processed NASA MERRA-2 monthly data (2014-2025) for four variables: temperature, precipitation, humidity, and wind. The site shows an explorable 3D globe of trends on a 5° grid, plus country views, city-level values from the nearest ~50 km grid cell, regional comparisons, and a ranking of the strongest significant changes. Each place has a yearly chart, a trend slope, a p-value, and a clear “significant / not significant” badge.

It addresses the challenge by making variable selection simple and by revealing opposite trends in different regions, even for the same variable. It is important because it helps students, educators, and the public read climate trends honestly. We state the limits openly: the record is short, p-values are unadjusted, and reanalysis is model-assisted. An SI assistant answers general space questions and is labeled as SI-generated.
details:
What it does and how it works

Sherlock Earth is an interactive 3D globe that shows how Earth's climate has changed from 2014 to 2025. It answers four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the trend is statistically real.

Users pick an indicator (temperature, precipitation, humidity, or wind) and see the globe colored by trend. The globe is divided into 5° grid cells, 2,592 in total. Each cell's color is the slope of a linear regression through its annual values. Blue means decreasing and red means increasing, on a scale centered on zero. A dot marks cells where the trend is statistically significant (p < 0.05), and non-significant cells are faded.

Users can click any cell, search for a country or city, or compare places. A side panel then shows:

  • the estimated trend and its p-value
  • an annual time series with the fitted line
  • all four indicators for the same location
  • a global area-weighted average for context

The site also has an onboard SI agent. You give it a goal, such as "Where is warming fastest?", and it plans steps over the project's data and moves the globe and panels to show the answer. It reads only the precomputed data, so it never invents numbers. There are also optional live layers: current temperature from Open-Meteo and satellite imagery from NASA GIBS.

Benefits

  • It makes raw climate reanalysis data understandable to students, educators, and the general public without any technical background.
  • It shows uncertainty openly. Significance markers, faded cells, and a "Read before you cite" note help users avoid over-reading short-term noise.
  • It works at several scales: global, regional, country, and city.
  • It runs in the browser with no installation, and every displayed value comes from a transparent, precomputed dataset.

Intended impact

The goal is to build data literacy about climate change, not just awareness. The site teaches people how to read a trend: what a slope is, what a p-value does and doesn't mean, why a 12-year record is short, and why a significant cell isn't proof of long-term change or causation. We want users to leave better able to question climate claims and to explore their own region's data.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, HTML/CSS, and React 19, built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS. Bun manages packages. A small Express (Node.js) server hosts the Gemini-powered space Q&A assistant through the Google GenAI SDK.
  • Visualization: globe.gl for the interactive 3D globe, Chart.js for the annual trend charts, Motion for animation, and Lucide for icons.
  • Hosting: Vercel, with the source on GitHub.
  • Data: NASA MERRA-2 (Modern-Era Retrospective analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2), covering 2014-2025. Country outlines and populated places come from Natural Earth. Live temperature comes from Open-Meteo, and true-color satellite imagery from NASA GIBS.
  • Processing: Our own scripts compute annual means (totals for precipitation), area-weighted averages, ordinary least-squares slopes, and p-values, and write them to a project JSON that the front end reads.
  • SI tools: Claude, Qoder, GitHub Copilot, and Google Antigravity helped with code and documentation. The in-app space Q&A assistant uses Gemini. The project idea, data choice, analysis design, and review of results were done by our team.
  • Hardware: Standard laptops, with no special hardware needed. The site runs on any modern browser.

How it's creative

  • Detective framing: The "Sherlock" idea turns climate data into a set of clues to investigate, not a wall of charts.
  • Honest visualization: Significance is shown by fading and markers, not just color. Each indicator has its own fixed color scale, because sharing one number across different units would imply a false equivalence.
  • Agent on the globe: The SI agent doesn't just answer in text. It plans steps, then focuses the Sahel, compares regions, or switches layers on the globe itself, while staying tied to real data.
  • Learning built in: An in-app "How to read Sherlock Earth" guide covers statistical caution, and the multiple-testing warning is stated plainly: with 2,592 cells, about 130 can look significant by chance alone.
  • Atmosphere: Night/Light modes, orbit controls, and a country mode make exploring feel like looking at a real planet.

Factors the team considered

  • Data quality: Reanalysis is model-assisted, not a station network, and the record is short, so we flagged these limits on the site.
  • Statistical rigor: We used OLS slopes with unadjusted p-values and said so openly, including the multiple-testing issue.
  • Accessibility and usability: The site is keyboard-friendly, has a skip link, and uses color scales centered on zero. It also works on mobile, since users can tap a cell and search by place name.
  • Transparency about AI: We disclosed which tools helped, labeled the Q&A assistant's answers as SI-generated, and kept it from creating or changing any data. No media is AI-generated and no NASA branding is used.
  • Scale and fairness: City values come from the nearest grid cell, so nearby cities can share a value. We documented that, along with the area-weighting choices for countries and regions.
